name: Jackson §14.6: the critical frequency
description: Jackson §14.6: the same receiver as before, but now it only counts angular frequencies from 80 to 160 (the shaded band of the spectrum in the panel). A bend's radiation reaches the receiver as a short flash, the shorter the tighter the bend, and a short flash contains high frequencies: up to about $\tfrac{3}{2}\gamma^3 c/R$ for a bend of radius R. A gentle bend that lit the receiver before may put almost nothing into this band: bend the particle harder, while it heads for the receiver, to deliver at least 0.003 per steradian in the band. Watch the spectrum move up as the bend gets tighter.

reality.represents: The critical frequency of synchrotron radiation (Jackson §14.6)

remarks.detail: A bend lights the receiver for a time of about R/(γ³c), so its spectrum reaches about (3/2)γ³c/R: why synchrotron light from tight bends of fast electrons reaches X-rays.

remarks.line: The radiation is exact for the motion
remarks.detail: What the receiver collects is computed from the particle's computed path with the exact far-zone fields (Liénard; the spectrum from Jackson's radiation integral), and the particle feels its radiation's reaction (Landau–Lifshitz).

c is 2 cells per time unit and the particle's γ is 3, so that its cone (1/γ, about 19°) and its flashes fit the board. Real synchrotron sources run electrons at γ in the thousands, beamed into fractions of a milliradian, out to X-rays.
The receiver averages over directions in the plane of the motion; the real radiation also goes out of the plane, where its pattern differs.
